title: Written under obedience
hookLine: someone you love asks for something you'd never choose; Thérèse's sister asked her to write her memories
tomorrow: why would a saint be glad to be a daisy and not a rose?

cards: Somebody you love asks for something you'd never have picked: record Grandpa's stories, make the slideshow for the anniversary, write down how the family got here. It feels like homework with feelings attached.

A young French nun named Thérèse got a request like that. Her older sister, who was also her prioress, asked her to write down her memories. So Thérèse knelt before a statue of Mary and prayed for help.
Then she opened the Gospel, and her eyes landed on one line.

teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims, Mark writes that Jesus, going up into a mountain, "called unto him whom he would himself." Thérèse reads it as the key to her life: not what she earned, but whom he chose to call.
So her book, Story of a Soul, doesn't open on a birth date. It opens on that line. First, obedience.
She didn't set out to write a book.
Mother Agnes, her own sister Pauline, asked, and Thérèse said yes.
In a Carmelite house a request from the prioress is something to obey, and she treats the writing that way: a small act of trust, not a project of her own. Second, the song.
She won't tell her life in the usual way, she says.
She'll sing the mercies of the Lord, borrowing the psalm: "The mercies of the Lord I will sing for ever." The memories are there to show what God did. Third, the flower.
She calls the pages the story of a little white flower, and the flower is herself. Fourth, the reader.
The pages are written to one person, the sister who asked.
Here's the thing to tell a friend: a book Catholics still read began as a notebook for one sister.

how: Catholics read Story of a Soul at home, in parish groups and in Carmelite communities, often slowly, a few pages at a time.

o: writing because a trusted superior asked
writing to obey a strict rule word for word
writing a life story as a kind of penance

games.q: written under obedience — tap the pairs.
p: her sister, who asked her to write
he called whom he would himself
the mercies of the Lord I will sing

s: written under obedience means she was forced to write against her will
her sister and prioress asked, and she said yes, as a small act of trust.
Story of a Soul opens on a line from Mark's Gospel, not on her birth date
he called unto him whom he would himself.
Thérèse wrote these first pages for the public
she wrote them to one person, the sister who asked.

games.q: your aunt asks you to give the toast at your grandparents' anniversary. your version is a timeline: dates, addresses, jobs. what would Thérèse's opening change?
o: open on what was given: the mercies, not the résumé.
add more dates, so nobody can say it's inaccurate.
hand it back; a toast you didn't choose won't ring true.
games.why: Thérèse refuses to tell her life the usual way. She sings the mercies of the Lord: the memories are there to show what was given.

practice: Take a page and write one memory by hand, not a date, a moment you'd call a gift. If someone has asked you for a story lately, start with theirs.
If you pray, you can begin with the psalm: the mercies of the Lord I will sing for ever.

wordCard.voice: Written under obedience. Thérèse began her book because someone she trusted asked, and she said yes.

orig.note: Latin for the mercies of the Lord, the psalm line Thérèse says she will sing.

carryVoice: Your line: the story of a soul. Not a résumé, a song of what was given. Until tomorrow.
